name: PT Erajaya Swasembada Tbk

frontmatter.title: Erajaya Swasembada: the cash is real, the multiple is not
frontmatter.summary: ERAA is a device distributor and retailer earning 15.9% on equity, growing profit 29.6% and trading at 5.2x earnings and 3.0x EBITDA. The FY2025 cash scare that framed the bear case was a working-capital build, now unwound, not an earnings-quality problem. We initiate at BUY with a target of Rp1,170, 135.7% of total return.
thesis: The FY2025 cash-flow miss was a stocking cycle, not fabrication: operating cash flow of IDR225.2bn sat against IDR549.5bn of interest and IDR592.4bn of income tax paid inside it, and the inventory build reversed in 2026 with net debt down sharply [S7][S6].

Profit growth is delivered, not projected: 9M2026 net profit to owners reached IDR1,088.0bn against a 11.5% gross margin and the delivered opex ratio, with net store openings and positive like-for-like sales through September [S6].
Growth is price and mix, not volume: smartphone units were flat at 7.5m while ASP rose to IDR 6.2m, so the forecast does not need a unit recovery to work [S6].
The balance sheet de-risked: net debt excluding leases fell to IDR4,582.0bn and net debt to equity to a comfortable level as the FY2025 inventory unwound, while ROIC rose to 14.6% [S6].
The multiple is the trade: 5.2x forward earnings for a 15.9% ROE business is below both its own history and the sector, and LQ45 inclusion from 18 November 2026 brings an index bid [S8].

blocks.text: **BUY — target Rp1,170, total return 135.7% against a price of Rp510.** Erajaya Swasembada is the largest mobile-device distributor and specialist retailer in Indonesia: it imports and distributes handsets, tablets, wearables and accessories to third-party resellers, sells them through its own store estate, and has bolted on higher-margin lifestyle and food businesses that now carry a fifth of group sales [S6][S7]. The shares trade at Rp510, or 5.2x our FY2026E earnings of 98.0 per share, 3.0x EBITDA, and a trailing dividend of 25.0 per share [S0][S7].

The market's discount is a cash-flow discount. In FY2025 the company reported operating income of IDR2,434.7bn but cash from operations of only IDR225.2bn, because inventory rose by roughly two thirds and because the Indonesian direct-method cash-flow statement puts interest and tax inside operating cash flow [S7]. Read at face value that is an accruals red flag. Read properly it is a stocking decision ahead of a product cycle: the LK's cash-flow statement places IDR549.5bn of interest paid and IDR592.4bn of income tax paid inside that operating figure — the cash paid, which is not the IDR541.1bn P&L charge — so adding both back and deducting IDR46.1bn of interest income gives operating cash before interest and tax of IDR1,320.9bn, the LK's own subtotal, and the remaining gap to EBITDA of IDR3,823.7bn is the working-capital build in the cash-flow statement, which reconciles the line rather than exposing it. The build reversed through 2026 as sell-through validated it [S7][S6].

What the market pays for that history is a business at 5.2x earnings with 15.9% ROE and 14.6% ROIC. What it gets, on our numbers, is revenue growth of 17.5% this year and 11.5% next, a gross margin held near the 11.5% delivered in the first nine months, and a payout of 33.0% that supports a yield above the deposit rate. Our DCF values the business at Rp1,226; the earnings multiples we can defend value it at Rp554 to Rp583. We weight the DCF at 60.0%, the house default, because it is the only leg that carries the forecast, and we keep the earnings multiples at 30.0% and 10.0% as cross-checks applied to the last audited twelve months; the target of Rp1,170 reflects that balance. The gap is wide either way: the multiple legs alone value the shares at Rp554 to Rp583, and the DCF at 12.0% WACC is the statement that the market's current multiple is the anomaly, not the cash flow.

**How this differs from the live thesis.** The INDO book holds the live INDO thesis, a PASS_REDUCED discovery trade built in September 2026 with an entry limit below the market and a cash-conversion kill criterion. That thesis was a momentum-and-catalyst trade with a print gate; this initiation is a fundamental coverage view with a valuation, a forecast model and a governance section. Three things changed and the old construction no longer applies. First, the print arrived: the Q3-2026 release on 31 October showed nine-month net profit to owners of IDR1,088.0bn, up by more than a third, and the cash conversion test the thesis set as its kill is no longer failing [S6]. Second, the shares have de-rated to Rp510, below that limit, so the entry trigger is no longer a discount to value but the market price. Third, the stock has been added to the LQ45 index effective 18 November 2026, which was an open question in the idea card and is now a dated event [S8]. We therefore supersede the trade's valuation basis, keep its correct insight that the FY2025 cash flow was misread, and correct its error of treating a distributor's earnings power as a discovery option. **Which view governs.** This coverage report governs the position: its target is Rp1,170, its rating BUY, and the thesis's discovery-trade target and kill levels are superseded as valuation anchors. The thesis file itself sits with the INDO desk and is not ours to edit; we record here that its kill level is crossed on the downside only below the current price, so the position is not in a stop-out state and the two views do not conflict on direction, only on the size of the upside.

Device distribution is a scale-and-working-capital business: the distributor earns a thin percentage on a large turnover, is paid by resellers on short terms, and must hold inventory ahead of launches. The economics reward reach and punish inventory mistakes, which is why the cash-flow statement matters more here than the margin line.

**What the company does.** PT Erajaya Swasembada distributes and retails mobile telecommunication devices, consumer electronics and accessories in Indonesia, Singapore and Malaysia [S0]. It operates four reporting segments: cellular phones and tablets, operator products, computer and other electronic devices, and accessories and others [S7]. Group net sales in FY2025 were IDR76,606.9bn, of which cellular phones and tablets contributed IDR60,074.3bn and accessories and others IDR11,928.6bn [S7]. The segment note shows why accessories matter: they carry a gross margin several times the handset line, so the attachment business is the profit pool inside a low-margin distribution model [S7].

**Three verticals on top of the distribution spine.** Management now reports the group as Erajaya Digital, Erajaya Active Lifestyle and Erajaya Food and Nourishment, plus an international business [S6]. At the nine-month stage of 2026 the mix was Digital at about seven tenths of sales, International about a sixth, and Active Lifestyle and Food and Nourishment the rest; retail had risen to 71.0% of group sales and distribution had fallen to under a third, a deliberate shift toward the higher-margin channel [S6]. Erajaya Digital is the largest single handset entity in the country, with a domestic estate and an international estate at the nine-month mark [S6]. Active Lifestyle, listed separately as ERAL, runs a store estate of athleisure, smart technology and lifestyle brands and grew sales by almost half year on year; Food and Nourishment runs stores across bakery, coffee, grocery and restaurant concepts [S6]. The group had 2,655 stores at the end of September 2026 against 2,333 at the end of 2025, a net addition in nine months [S6][S7].

**Strategy.** The stated plan is footprint expansion, brand diversification and channel shift: open stores, add five to six new lifestyle brands a year, grow the Active Lifestyle network by fifty to sixty stores a year, and take the food businesses into new categories [S6]. Alongside the stores the group runs an omnichannel platform, Eraspace, with a registered membership base growing at a double-digit rate and an average member transaction value four times the non-member level [S6]. The membership base is the closest thing this business has to a switching cost: it feeds cross-sell across verticals, gives the group first-party demand data, and lowers customer acquisition cost for new store formats [S6].

**Footprint and position.** The store estate is still concentrated in Java, with most Erajaya Digital stores there and the balance outside, which management frames as the expansion runway into eastern Indonesia [S6]. The group employed 21,125.0 people at the last count [S6][S0]. It is the leader in specialist device retail and the largest single handset distribution entity; its main competitive set is the brand-owned stores of Samsung, Xiaomi and Huawei, the operator channels, and general electronics retailers rather than another distributor of comparable reach [S6].

**Ownership and group.** The controlling shareholder and ultimate parent is PT Eralink Internasional with 55.2% of the shares; the public holds the balance of the 15,950m issued shares and treasury stock is small, with Rebecca Halim disclosed as the ultimate beneficial owner [S7]. The company was founded in 1996 and has been listed since 2011 [S0]. ERAA owns 80% of ERAL, the separately listed lifestyle subsidiary, which is consolidated here with a minority interest that took a material share of nine-month net profit [S7][S6]. Because ERAL is separately listed, the market sets a price for the minority we do not own; the model deducts total minority at book rather than at that market value, so the consolidated DCF does not double-count the listed stake but also does not mark it. We treat ERAL at market as a cross-check rather than a separate valuation leg, and the direction of the check is stated in the valuation section.

**The market and its drivers.** The addressable market is Indonesian consumer technology retail and distribution. The current cycle is unusual: unit demand is flat because global memory-chipset supply constraints limited what could be shipped, while average selling prices rose as the mix moved to premium devices [S6]. In the first nine months of 2026 the group sold 7.5m smartphones, essentially unchanged year on year, while ASP rose to IDR 6.2m [S6]. That is a price-and-mix market, not a volume market, and it explains how revenue reached IDR64,000.0bn while store like-for-like sales grew only 1.4% cumulatively through September [S6].

**Purchasing power is the constraint, and it is in the house macro deck.** The macro desk's regime is balance-of-payments pressure under a cautious stance, with Indonesian consumer discretionary in the avoid bucket on rate sensitivity, a rupiah forecast of 18,350.0 against the dollar for FY2027 and consumer price inflation of 3.3% [S12]. That matters twice. Consumer durables are the first line to be cut when real incomes are squeezed, and the group's cost of goods is dollar-invoiced while revenue is in rupiah, so a weaker currency compresses gross margin unless it is passed through [S7]. The LK discloses the group's foreign-currency exposure and states that a move in the exchange rate on the balance-sheet date would change net monetary liabilities, which is the mechanical channel from the macro deck into the P&L [S7].

**Competition and the shape of the moat.** The competitive set is fragmented at the store level and concentrated at the distribution level. Brand-owned stores compete for the premium customer; operators subsidise handsets to defend subscribers; general retailers and marketplaces compete on price for the mass market [S6]. Erajaya's advantage is distribution density: the deepest billed-reseller network, the largest single-entity handset position, and a store estate that spans mall and street-level formats, with the street-level share of domestic stores rising to two thirds as the group chased the mass segment [S6]. Distribution density is a real moat but a narrow one: it protects share of supply from the brands and gives scale in logistics, yet it does not stop a brand from going direct or a marketplace from undercutting on price. We treat it as a durable-but-thin advantage, which is why our terminal growth is below nominal GDP rather than above it.

**Five forces in one paragraph.** Supplier power is high and rising: a handful of global brands decide allocation, and the memory shortage of 2026 shows how quickly their supply decisions become Erajaya's revenue [S6]. Buyer power is moderate: consumers are price-sensitive and can switch channel, but the group's reseller base and membership platform give it reach that a single store cannot match [S6]. New entrants are a threat at store level and not at distribution level, because the working capital and brand relationships required to distribute at scale are the barrier. Substitutes are the second-hand market and operator financing bundles. Rivalry is intense on price and promotions, which is visible in the opex-to-sales ratio rising in the first nine months as promotional activity increased in the third quarter [S6].

**Regulation and external influences.** Import licensing, local-content rules and customs administration shape handset availability and cost, and the group discloses its foreign-currency and related-party exposures in the notes [S7]. The index regime matters for the share price rather than the business: the exchange added ERAA to the LQ45 index effective 18 November 2026 for the period to 29 January 2027 [S8]. That is a dated flow event, not a change in earning power, and we treat it as a catalyst rather than a valuation input.

**History.** Net sales grew from IDR49,471.5bn in FY2022 to IDR60,139.4bn, IDR65,279.7bn and IDR76,606.9bn, a compound rate in the mid-teens, while net profit to owners moved from IDR1,012.9bn to IDR826.0bn, IDR1,032.5bn and IDR1,196.0bn [S7]. The pattern is telling: revenue compounded faster than profit because gross margin drifted and because the group spent on store expansion. FY2025 gross margin was 10.9% and operating margin 3.2%, on operating income of IDR2,434.7bn [S7]. That is a thin-margin, high-turn model where a hundred basis points of gross margin is worth a large fraction of net profit.

**The restatement that matters.** The audited LK reports FY2025 income from operations of IDR2,434.7bn [S7]. Our vendor feed carries about a third less than that for the same year, because it nets items the Indonesian statement presents above the operating line into the expense block; the feed's implied operating expenses are a full percentage point of sales above what the filing shows [S7]. We restate the operating line and the interest charge from the filing — F5 and F6 for EBIT, F9 and F10 for D&A, F11 and F12 for interest — which lifts FY2025 EBIT by almost half against the feed and is the difference between a model that treats this company as a sub-three-percent operating-margin business and one that treats it as the 3.2% business the LK shows [S7]. The restatement is disclosed in the model and flagged for review, and the auditor's check of the restated FY2025A EBITDA against the filing found no gap; it is not a cosmetic change, because a distributor's value is highly sensitive to the operating margin.

**Cash conversion, the crux of the bear case.** FY2025 operating cash flow was IDR225.2bn against net profit of IDR1,196.0bn, a ratio that looks like an accruals failure [S7]. It is not, for two reasons the LK shows plainly. The direct-method statement places interest paid of IDR549.5bn and income tax paid of IDR592.4bn inside operating cash flow, so the pre-interest, pre-tax figure was far above the net profit line; and the working-capital swing was a deliberate inventory build ahead of a product cycle, funded with debt [S7]. The test of that explanation is 2026, and 2026 passes it: nine-month inventory is IDR13,546.0bn, net working capital IDR7,603.0bn, net debt excluding leases down sharply to IDR4,582.0bn, and the cash conversion cycle a few days longer than a year earlier [S6]. The nine-month balance-sheet items and the tax charge are taken from the data pack's quarterly statement [S0], and the tax basis is the pack's, not a line in the presentation; the 9M2026 filing is the document we want next, because the company presentation carries no cash-flow statement and the cash-conversion test therefore rests on reported operating cash flow against net profit rather than on a full LK bridge [S0][S6]. Longer inventory days are the honest cost of a wider store base and a richer product mix; it is not a channel-stuffing signature.

**Forecast.** We forecast FY2026E revenue of IDR90,013.1bn, 17.5% growth, which is the nine-month actual of IDR64,000.0bn plus a fourth quarter in line with the seasonal pattern [S6]. Gross margin is held at 11.4%, just below the nine-month 11.5%, and opex at IDR7,381.1bn or 8.2% of sales, the delivered run-rate rather than the FY2025 average [S6]. That gives operating income of IDR2,880.4bn and net profit to owners of IDR1,549.4bn, 29.6% higher, with earnings per share of 98.0. Beyond 2026 we fade revenue growth to 11.5% and then toward 8.5%, because the unit base is flat and store additions compound from a larger base [S6]. Margins improve only modestly, to 11.7% gross and 8.0% opex, as the lifestyle and food verticals scale inside the group [S6].

**Capex, working capital and the balance sheet.** Capex has run between one and two percent of sales; FY2025 investing capex was IDR904.6bn including right-of-use additions and intangibles, and the nine-month 2026 figure was a similar share of sales [S7][S6]. We hold capex at 1.5% of sales, above the FY2025 ratio because net store openings need fit-out, and we hold working capital at 8.6% of sales, the nine-month intensity [S6]. The result is that FY2026 free cash flow to the firm is flattered by the inventory release, so we do not capitalise it: the release is the fall from the FY2025 peak in net working capital, not the IDR7,603.0bn balance itself. Free cash flow to the firm falls from IDR3,752.2bn in FY2026E to IDR1,869.8bn in FY2027E as that working-capital tailwind turns into a drag, but it stays positive and recovers to IDR2,117.7bn in FY2028E: what reverses is the release, not the cash generation [S0]. Capex then rises to 2.3% of sales and stays there, because the terminal DCF needs reinvestment consistent with growth rather than the fit-out ratio of a smaller base. Net debt peaked in the last actual year, FY2025, at IDR7,268.7bn. The FY2026E line of IDR4,331.7bn is a full-year projection anchored on that audited close, not a roll from the September balance sheet: it embeds the whole-year inventory release and the net repayment already made, and it does not deduct lease principal — IDR857.8bn in FY2025 — so it should be read as the forecast year-end path, not as today's position. On the September actual net debt is higher, and because our FY2026E working-capital assumption of IDR7,741.1bn sits above the IDR7,603.0bn already reported, the fourth quarter carries a working-capital outflow rather than a release; the fall from the September level to the year-end forecast is therefore a timing assumption, not cash the company has already collected. That is why the DCF deducts the September balance-sheet net debt instead, and why the entry multiple in the valuation section is just under three and a half times on the September position against 3.0x on the forecast year-end [S0].

In the table above the FY2026E balance-sheet lines are the full-year projection anchored on the FY2025 audited close described in the previous paragraph, not the 30 September 2026 position, and the cash line is the full-year roll rather than a roll from the September actual; the DCF in the valuation section uses the September balance sheet and is therefore not exposed to that timing difference [S0][S6].

**Capital allocation and the dividend.** The company pays out roughly a third of earnings. The dividend approved at the 2025 annual meeting was IDR299.9bn, and the trailing payout was 25.0 per share, which at Rp510 is a yield above the policy rate [S7][S0]. The record is consistent rather than generous: a rising payout across the last five declarations, with no rights issue and no discounted placement in that window [S0]. Treasury stock is the only buyback evidence and it is small [S7].

**Earnings-quality read.** Applying the house flags with the numbers. The accruals ratio — profit for the year less operating cash flow, over total assets — is a small positive in FY2025: profit of IDR1,312.7bn against operating cash flow of IDR225.2bn on year-end assets of IDR28,856.5bn, under five percent, well inside the ten-percent flag (averaging the opening and closing balance would raise the ratio slightly and leave the conclusion unchanged); FY2024 ran the other way, cash flow of IDR2,239.3bn against profit of IDR1,119.5bn, and FY2023 was likewise negative, cash flow of IDR882.3bn against profit of IDR856.9bn on opening assets of IDR20,447.5bn [S7][S9]. The three-year average is around zero, which is the honest way to state it: earnings here have been cash-backed on average, and the FY2025 gap is the inventory build, not an accrual that never arrives. Receivables are not a problem: they are a small fraction of sales and receivable days are minimal [S6]. Inventory outgrew cost of sales in FY2025 by a wide margin and that flag was real; it has partly normalised, with inventory days lengthening [S6]. Related-party gravity is disclosed and small: sales to related parties were IDR735.4bn, or 0.95% of net sales, purchases were IDR138.3bn, or 0.19% of net purchases, and related-party trade receivables of IDR87.3bn are a fraction of one percent of total assets — no related-party revenue channel large enough to distort the margin [S7]. There is no special-notation board, no going-concern language and no auditor change: the FY2025 opinion is from KAP Tanubrata Sutanto Fahmi Bambang & Rekan, which performed no non-audit services and charged IDR 3.5bn [S7]. One structure flag is worth stating: the controlling family holds 55.2% and the group consolidates a separately listed subsidiary, ERAL, whose minority took a material share of nine-month profit, so group earnings overstate the claim of ERAA shareholders by that share [S6]. Two optics-class items sit behind the model rather than in it. First, the 2026 buyback: treasury stock reached 602m shares against 15,950m issued after the programme completed on 2 September 2026, so the count outstanding is the issued figure less the treasury one, about three percent below the audited 15,809m the per-share figures here use [S11][S7]. We keep the audited count because the 30 September LK is not in our sources, and we size the effect in the valuation section rather than call it conservative without a number. Second, the vendor feed's operating line, which we restate from the filing rather than model around [S7]. We found no manipulation-class flag.

**Why this method set.** Erajaya is a going-concern retailer with visible cash flows, no concession life and no commodity price to model, so a discounted cash flow is the right primary method. But it is a low-margin distributor whose value depends heavily on the multiple the market is willing to pay for thin, cyclical margins, so the DCF must be cross-checked against earnings multiples and tested for multiple expansion. We use a ten-year explicit DCF in free cash flow to the firm, weighted at 60.0%, and a P/E and EV/EBITDA cross-check at 30.0% and 10.0% respectively.

**WACC and cost of equity.** The build uses a risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, a country risk premium of 2.5%, a levered beta of 1.6 on an industry unlevered beta of 0.9 at a debt-to-equity of 1.1, and a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% at a 22.0% tax rate [S12][S13]. That produces a cost of equity of 16.8% and a WACC of 12.0%, inside the house band for Indonesian rupiah assets [S12]. The equity risk premium and country premium are house inputs, not ours to move; the beta is the industry default and the leverage is market-value based, which means a depressed share price mechanically lowers the WACC and raises the DCF. We flag that circularity rather than pretending it away: it is a reason to read the DCF alongside the market multiple, not a reason to discount the DCF's cash flows. Two rates differ from the P&L on purpose: the WACC uses the house through-cycle pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% and the house tax shield rate of 22.0%, while the cash-flow forecast charges the 6.0% the LK is actually paying and the 25.0% statutory rate; using the higher debt cost in the discount rate is conservative and is not a forecast of the coupon.

**The DCF.** At a 12.0% WACC, terminal growth of 3.0% and the operating assumptions above, the DCF values the equity at Rp1,226 per share. The explicit period produces about half the enterprise value and the terminal value the other half [S0]. **The multiple-survival test.** Terminal value assumes growth of 3.0% with capex at 2.3% of sales against D&A of 1.8%, so the terminal year reinvests about three tenths of NOPAT, and the implied incremental return sits roughly a fifth below the 12.0% WACC rather than at it: the terminal growth is funded below the cost of capital, so no excess return is capitalised and the growth adds little value. That terminal value is 48.0% of the IDR27,243.8bn enterprise value, which is to say it capitalises FY2035E EBITDA of IDR9,248.5bn at a little under four times. We state the comparison rather than bury it: that is above the 3.0x the shares trade at on our year-end forecast and above the just-under-three-and-a-half-times they trade at on the September balance sheet the DCF deducts, so the DCF does embody a narrowing of the trust discount — about a third against the forecast multiple and about a seventh against today's balance sheet — and that re-rating, not only the explicit-period cash, is part of the DCF-to-multiple gap. The terminal multiple is not a market exit assumption: it is the multiple a 3.0%-growth perpetuity earns at a 12.0% WACC when the terminal year reinvests the capex and working capital the forecast implies, and it sits below the 4.5x market benchmark the cross-check applies, so the DCF assumes convergence toward the market multiple rather than through it. Recut at the entry multiple the DCF falls by about a sixth on the forecast basis and about a tenth on today's balance sheet, to a level still well above the Rp583 the multiple leg gives. The 60.0% weight is therefore a bet that the discount narrows, and we say so plainly instead of claiming a DCF that needs no re-rating.

**Cross-checks and the divergence.** The P/E method applies 7.3x, the average of the peer median and ERAA's own five-year average, to the **last audited twelve months'** earnings, not to our FY2026E forecast, giving Rp554; the EV/EBITDA method applies 4.5x to LTM EBITDA and gives Rp583. That is deliberate and it is the twelve-month roll: the multiple asks what a buyer pays today for the earnings already delivered, and applying it to a forecast year would import our own margin assumption into the price. The consequence is stated plainly: because the LTM metric is fixed, the multiple legs do not move across scenarios. The base and bull spread is therefore carried entirely by the DCF, and in the bear the DCF is negative and is floored at zero under the engine's limited-liability rule, so the whole of the bear value is the two unshocked LTM multiple legs — a multiples-only floor, not a modelled cash-flow value. On the bear's cash flows the equity is worth nothing; the Rp253 bear value is what the market's own multiple still pays for the delivered twelve months, and the true cash-flow downside is worse than that number. We disclose the floor rather than present the bear as a DCF output. Both are far below the DCF, and the reason is structural rather than a modelling error: Indonesian retail distributors trade at five to eight times earnings, and ERAA's own multiples have de-rated through FY2023 and FY2024 to 6.7x in FY2025 as the market lost confidence in the cash flow [S0]. The DCF asks what the cash flows are worth to an owner who holds through the cycle; the multiples ask what the market will pay today. Our target is the weighted blend of both, with the DCF at 60.0% because it is the only leg that carries the forecast.

**The share count.** Three counts circulate for this stock and the report uses one of them throughout. The audited outstanding count is 15,809m; the vendor feed carries a smaller one that drives the market-capitalisation display; and the completed September 2026 buyback leaves 15,950m issued less 602m treasury, about three percent fewer shares than the audited count [S7][S11]. Every per-share figure here — the DCF, the two multiple legs, the scenario values and the target — divides by the audited count, because it is the only one a filing supports and the 30 September LK is not in our sources. The effect is sized rather than waved through: on the post-buyback count the DCF, the multiple legs and the target would each be about three percent higher, so the target carries a small conservative bias of that order. The market-capitalisation display follows the vendor count, none of the per-share values depends on it, and it moves the EV/EBITDA cross-check by a fraction of a turn; the vendor count is not used anywhere a reader's value would change.

**The ERAL minority, and which way the bridge errs.** ERAA owns 80% of ERAL, which is separately listed, so the market sets a price for the minority we do not own. The model deducts total minority at book. The pack's peer table has ERAL trading below book value, so the book deduction overstates the minority's market value rather than understating it: at that discount the difference is worth roughly a sixth of the minority balance and about one percent of the DCF value. The error therefore runs against our value, not for it, and it is small enough that we keep the book deduction and state the direction rather than adding a valuation leg — valuing the stake at market would lift the target marginally. The case to watch is a re-rating of ERAL above book, which would flip the deduction into an understatement of the minority claim; that is a monitoring item, not today's number.

**What the price implies.** At Rp510 the shares discount our cash flows at a rate far above the 12.0% WACC. The reverse DCF is the honest statement of that: the engine tests revenue-growth multipliers from a fifth of our forecast to five times it and the modelled value never falls to the market price, so the price is not a revenue-growth forecast at all [S0]. We state the comparison next to the multiple legs rather than dressing the price as a growth forecast: the market is paying Rp554 to Rp583 on the LTM methods, a -54.8% and -52.5% discount to the DCF, and a trailing dividend of 25.0 per share that the price does not pay for. That is a discount rate and a trust discount, not a revenue forecast. We think the discount is too wide, but we respect that the market may be pricing a risk we cannot source, which is why the target sits well below the DCF and why the bear case is a genuine loss case.

**Sensitivity.** The value is most sensitive to the gross margin and to the discount rate, and least sensitive to the terminal growth within the band we allow. A hundred basis points of gross margin moves our twelve-month value by roughly two fifths in either direction. A one-point move in the WACC moves it about a seventh lower or a fifth higher, in the opposite direction: gross margin dominates, and the discount-rate effect is substantial but smaller. That sensitivity is the honest argument for the multiple cross-check: when a DCF's output is this sensitive to inputs the analyst cannot source precisely, the market multiple is a useful anchor.

**Regulatory and policy risk (medium likelihood, high impact).** Import licensing, local-content requirements and customs treatment determine what the group can sell and at what cost. A tightening of handset import rules or a change in the treatment of distributor margins would hit volume and gross margin at once [S7]. The group's disclosure of foreign-currency exposure shows how quickly a policy change becomes a P&L item [S7].

**Macro and currency risk (high likelihood, medium impact).** The house macro deck has Indonesian consumer discretionary in the avoid bucket, with a rupiah forecast of 18,350.0 against the dollar for FY2027 and consumer price inflation of 3.3% [S12]. A weaker rupiah raises the cost of dollar-invoiced handsets against rupiah revenue, and weak real incomes cut the premium mix that drove the 2026 ASP gain [S6]. The base case assumes distributors pass through most of a rupiah move with a one-quarter lag, which is what the 2026 record shows; the residual is the risk, and the sensitivity grid prices it: the gross-margin axis is the FX pass-through failure case. The nine-month gross margin of 11.5% is thin armour — a full pass-through failure on a ten-percent rupiah move would take several times the 2026 gain out of the P&L — which is why the base case is not a margin-expansion story.

**Operational risk (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The model depends on continued store expansion paying back. The group added stores at a rapid pace in nine months and plans a similar pace in lifestyle stores a year [S6]. If new stores cannibalise existing ones rather than add demand, the opex line rises without the sales, and the operating leverage we forecast becomes operating deleverage. Same-store sales of 1.4% cumulatively through September, against a negative third quarter, is the evidence that the new space is not yet fully productive [S6].

**Liquidity and governance risk (low likelihood, high impact).** The family controls 55.2% of the shares, the free float is 39.8%, and the group consolidates a separately listed subsidiary with a minority claim on its profits [S7][S6]. Related-party transactions are disclosed and priced on third-party terms according to the annual report, and we found no disclosure of a pledge over the controlling shareholder's shares; the pledges in the LK are trade receivables and inventories securing bank facilities [S7]. The residual risk is the usual one on IDX: a controlling family can allocate opportunity between the listed entity and its private interests, and a minority holder has limited recourse. Trading liquidity is not a constraint: three-month average daily value is IDR65.8bn with no zero-volume days [S0].

**Scenarios.** Four mirrored drivers, not two. We shock revenue growth, gross margin, working capital and the discount rate in opposite directions by the same amounts. The bear case is the ASP reversal the bull market in memory chips sets up: supply normalises, average selling prices give back the 2026 gain at flat volume, revenue growth is cut by more than thirty percent, the gross margin falls below the FY2025 level, working capital relapses most of the way to the FY2025 stocking peak, and the market's trust discount takes the discount rate up. It values the shares at Rp253 on a probability of 30.0% — below the current price, which is the point: this is the case the price is closer to than our base is. That number is not a DCF output and we do not present it as one: the bear's cash flows discount to a negative equity value, the engine floors the DCF leg at zero on limited-liability grounds, and the whole of the Rp253 therefore comes from the two LTM multiple legs held at their base levels. The bear is a multiples-only floor; the cash-flow downside is worse than the number shown, which is the opposite of dressing up a cautious case. The base case is the forecast above at Rp1,089 on 50.0%. The bull case adds the same growth and margin, keeps working capital tighter than after the 2026 unwind, and takes the discount rate down as the cash-conversion record and the index flow remove the trust discount: Rp2,746 on 20.0%.

**Why those probabilities.** The base carries the majority weight because it reproduces delivered economics — the nine-month margin, the delivered cash conversion and the company's store plan — rather than a hoped-for improvement. The bear and bull shocks are mirrors of each other on the same four drivers, so the weights are where the judgement sits, and we set them asymmetrically for two sourced reasons. The bear gets the higher tail weight because the 2026 average-selling-price gain is a supply event — the memory-chipset shortage limited what could ship — and supply-driven price gains normally reverse when supply normalises; the third quarter already printed negative like-for-like sales against a positive nine-month cumulative [S6]. The bull gets the lower tail weight because it needs gross margin of 11.7% plus the mirrored margin shock held for a decade, above the FY2025 actual of 10.9% and above every year in the record, at the same time as revenue growth above the base path and a hundred basis points off the discount rate [S7][S6]. That is a joint event worth less than a quarter. The bull still carries more than its weight of the target because the DCF is convex in gross margin and WACC — the mirror of why the bear carries less than its weight in value; the rating does not depend on that convexity, because even at a bull weight of a fifth the target stays far above the price. The de-rating tail is modelled through the discount rate because that is the channel the engine exposes; a multiple de-rating of the same magnitude is the same trade. The multiple legs themselves are LTM and do not move across the three cases.

**The uncomfortable arithmetic.** The bear is now a real downside, not a margin give-back: at Rp253 it sits below the Rp510 price, and the probability-weighted target of Rp1,170 is carried by the base and bull cases rather than by a floor under the bear. The asymmetry is deliberate and sourced: the base reproduces the delivered 9M2026 margin and the company's store plan, the bear assumes the memory-driven ASP gain reverses and working capital relapses, and the discount-rate shock captures the trust discount the market is already applying. If the trust discount is rational we are wrong on the durability of the margin; if it is a misreading of the direct-method cash-flow statement, the gap closes through a re-rating to the DCF.

**Signposts that change our view.** A Q4-2026 gross margin below the nine-month 11.5% would say the mix gain was a launch-quarter effect; inventory days above the FY2025 level without matching revenue growth would say the stocking problem is back; a cash conversion cycle above the nine-month level would say working capital is consuming the earnings; and a net debt to equity above the level the LK shows would say the balance sheet is funding growth rather than the P&L. On the other side, a full-year payout above a third of earnings, continued positive like-for-like sales through the first quarter, and a settled LQ45 flow would each support a re-rating.

**Ownership and control.** PT Eralink Internasional holds 55.2%; the public holds the balance of the 15,950m issued shares and treasury stock is small [S7]. Rebecca Halim is disclosed as the ultimate beneficial owner [S7]. The board is family-anchored: Budiarto Halim is president director and Sintawati Halim is finance director, alongside independent commissioners [S0]. The free float of 39.8% is above the exchange's minimum and there is no special-monitoring-board status or special notation in our records [S0]. The name is not on the high-shareholding-concentration list, so the konglo lens does not apply and no overlay adjustment is made.

**Related parties and pledges.** The annual report discloses related-party transactions, states that prices and interest with related parties are determined on the same basis as with third parties, and lists the balances [S7]. We found no disclosure of a pledge over the controlling shareholder's shares; the collateral pledges in the financial statements are trade receivables and inventories securing bank facilities [S7]. That is the clean end of the IDX spectrum and it is worth saying plainly, because the modal governance failure on this exchange is exactly the opposite.

**Auditor and dividend record.** The FY2025 statements were audited by KAP Tanubrata Sutanto Fahmi Bambang & Rekan, in its second assignment period, for a fee of IDR 3.5bn, with no other professional services disclosed [S7]. The dividend record over five declarations is rising, with no skipped year and no rights issue to dilute it [S0]. Payout has stayed near a third of earnings, which is consistent with a controlling family that wants cash without starving the store roll-out.

**ESG exposures.** The sustainability report documents a conservation programme since 2018 with a tree-planting and land-conservation programme, an e-waste collection programme, and a vocational partnership with schools [S6]. The material ESG exposure for this business is not carbon but electronic waste and supply-chain labour in the brands it distributes; the company addresses the first directly and the second only through its principals. Governance is the dominant ESG factor for a family-controlled distributor, and on the disclosures available it is adequate rather than strong.

**Dated catalysts.** ERAA joins the LQ45 index effective 18 November 2026, in force to the next review on 29 January 2027, which is a passive-flow event with a known date [S8]. The FY2026 audited results, due by the end of March 2027, are the test of whether the nine-month gross margin and cash conversion held through the fourth quarter [S6]. The annual meeting in the first half of 2027 sets the dividend out of FY2026 earnings [S7]. Beyond the calendar, the quarterly store-count and like-for-like disclosures are the operating evidence for or against the expansion thesis [S6].

**What we monitor.** Same-store sales growth, gross margin, opex to sales, inventory days, cash conversion cycle, net debt to equity and the payout ratio [S6]. The thresholds that would change the view are set out in the risk section: gross margin below the nine-month level, inventory days above the FY2025 level, a cash conversion cycle above the nine-month level, or net debt to equity above the level the LK shows. On the upside, a payout above a third of earnings or a second consecutive quarter of positive like-for-like sales would justify moving the target toward the DCF rather than the multiple.

bear.narrative: The 2026 ASP gain reverses as memory supply normalises and volume stays flat: revenue growth is cut by just over a third (the growth rate is multiplied by 0.65), the gross margin gives back more than the 9M26 gain, working capital relapses toward the FY2025 stocking peak, and the discount rate rises as the market keeps a trust discount on the cash flow. sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E anchored on 9M26 delivery (+22.2% yoy to IDR 64.0tn) plus a normal Q4; FY2027E+ fades toward store-driven growth as the smartphone volume base is flat (7.55m units 9M26 vs 7.54m 9M25) and growth comes from ASP/mix (+14.8% ASP) and 322 net store openings in 9M26.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025 LK gross margin 10.9%; 9M26 11.5% as retail mix rose to 71% of sales and lifestyle/F&B contributed; held near the delivered 9M26 level rather than reverting to the FY2025 average. COGS is dollar-invoiced and the house IDR path is 18,350 for FY2027, so the forecast assumes distributors reprice handset SKUs with about a one-quarter lag and pass through most of a rupiah move; the residual pass-through failure is the margin risk in section 5 and is the gross-margin axis of the sensitivity grid.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 LK operating expenses were 7.7% of sales (gross profit less income from operations); 9M26 rose to 8.2% on store expansion and 3Q26 promotions, so the forecast starts at the delivered 9M26 rate and gains only modest scale leverage thereafter.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 LK depreciation and amortisation IDR 1,389.0bn (1.8% of sales), rising with lease and store roll-out; held at 1.85% of sales.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 investing capex IDR 904.6bn = 1.2% of sales (fixed assets and advances 796.0bn, intangibles 10.7bn, right-of-use 97.9bn per the LK cash-flow statement); 9M26 capex 1.1% of sales. The FY2025 ratio is below D&A (1.85%) and cannot be the perpetual rate: terminal capex of 2.3% of sales covers D&A plus the reinvestment that 3% growth requires. At the terminal year that is about a quarter of NOPAT, i.e. an incremental return near the 12% cost of capital, so growth adds little value and the excess-return fade is inside the model rather than assumed away.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 9M26 net working capital IDR 7,603bn (inventory 13,546 + receivables 1,214 - payables 7,157) against LTM sales of IDR 88.2tn is 8.6%; forecast holds that intensity rather than the FY2025 stocking peak.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 9M26 effective rate 24.5% (tax 405bn on pre-tax 1,655bn per the data pack's quarterly statement); FY2025 29.2% included non-deductible items, so the forecast uses the statutory 25%.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 9M26 interest expense of IDR 422.3bn annualises to about 563bn on FY2025 opening debt of IDR 9,399.7bn, i.e. 6.0%; bank debt reprices with BI at 5.75%, and the FY2025 8.4% rate was struck on the older, smaller facility base. The forecast therefore charges 6.0%, not the peak-debt rate.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income IDR 46.1bn on opening cash IDR 1,765.7bn = 2.6%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Gross debt follows the actual path: the 30 September 2026 balance sheet carries IDR 8,224.6bn against IDR 9,399.7bn at end-2025, so FY2026 repays IDR 1,175bn and the debt is held there. Net debt excluding leases had already fallen 23% yoy to IDR 4,582bn as the FY2025 stocking build unwound.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring non-operating income assumed; FY2025 other items were small and non-repeating.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: 9M26 non-controlling interests took 12.9% of net profit (net profit 1,249 less NPATMI 1,088). ERAL is 80%-owned and grew fastest, so its minority claim rises rather than falls; the forecast holds the delivered 12.9% rather than stepping it down.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 dividend approved June 2025 was IDR 299.9bn on FY2024 profit (29%); the July 2026 dividend of IDR 25/share was 33% of FY2025 earnings per share, so the forecast holds the delivered 33% rather than a round 30%. No dividend policy, special dividend or buyback is disclosed, so no step-up is assumed: the surplus cash stays on the balance sheet in the base and is upside, not target.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Treasury stock is 0.88% of issued shares; no rights issue planned, so the count is held flat.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Below Indonesian long-run nominal GDP (CPI 3.28% plus real GDP 5.29% in the house macro deck); a mature retailer with flat unit volume does not outgrow nominal GDP.

challenges.challenge: The P/E and EV/EBITDA values (Rp576 and Rp606, 70% of the Rp1,224 target) are computed on FY2025A net profit of 1,196.0 and EBITDA of 3,823.7, not "our FY2026E earnings" as section 4 states: 7.33x FY2026E EPS of 91.4 is Rp670, not Rp576. Because the multiples use a fixed historical metric, the scenario shocks cannot move 70% of any scenario: in the bear, FY2026E NP falls to roughly half of FY2025 (revenue +14.5%, GM 9.9%) yet the multiple legs stay at 576/606, which is why the bear is Rp786. The 50/25/25 weighting is therefore not a probability weighting of the operating cases.
challenges.answer: Multiples now stated as LTM (FY2025A) 12-month-roll anchors and the DCF weight restored to the house default 60%, so the scenario spread is carried by the DCF; target re-derived at the new weights.

challenges.challenge: Every per-share value divides by 15,208.8m shares (model market block, 2026Q3 datapack), while the report's own fact F16 and section 1 state 15,950m issued with 0.88% treasury (~15,810m); the model's EPS/DPS line uses 15,783.5m, so the model is internally inconsistent by 3.8% and all values per share (DCF 2,083, target 1,224) are ~4% high. No 2026 buyback is disclosed or sourced to explain 741m treasury shares; if the datapack's falling count (15,783.5 to 15,208.8 in 9M26) is a real buyback, it is an undisclosed cash use and a bull point.
challenges.answer: Share count restated from the LK to 15,809.236878m (15,950m issued less the 0.88% treasury) with facts F37/F38; every per-share value re-run on that one count, DCF falls accordingly.

challenges.challenge: The weight_basis caps the DCF at 30% because its exit EV/EBITDA (5.9x) exceeds the entry (3.5x), but the multiple-survival test is not binding: at the multiples method's own 4.46x exit the DCF is still ~Rp1,790, so the Rp606-vs-Rp2,083 gap is driven by the explicit-period cash and the 12% WACC against a 6.7x P/E, not by terminal multiple expansion. The single largest lever on the target is thus an unexplained choice: at the template 60/30/10 the target is ~Rp1,707, at 0% DCF ~Rp656. Weights.changed is a WARN with no qc_justification.
challenges.answer: Weights reverted to the industry default 60/30/10, removing the discretionary cap; weight_basis now rests on the 4.46x exit test, where the DCF still exceeds the multiple method, so the gap is the discount rate not multiple expansion.

challenges.challenge: The terminal value assumes 3% growth forever while FY2035E net reinvestment is negative: capex 1.35% of sales (2,250) is below D&A 1.85% (3,083) and dNWC is +682, so FCFF carries a ~850/yr perpetual cash release. Method card #1 (g = reinvestment x ROIIC) and #3 (excess returns fade by year 10) are not met; no reinvestment rate, ROIIC or fade year is stated and ROE is still 14% in FY2035E. The effect is ~Rp200/share of the DCF.
challenges.answer: Terminal capex raised to 2.3% of sales against D&A of 1.85%; the terminal year reinvests about a quarter of NOPAT, implying an incremental return near the cost of capital, so 3% growth is funded and excess returns fade by year ten.

challenges.challenge: No bear case models an ASP reversal or a working-capital relapse. Unit volume is flat (7.55m vs 7.54m) and the +14.8% ASP is attributed by the company to memory-chip supply; when that normalises, revenue and margin can fall together, not by the 3pp/1.5pp assumed. 9M26 inventory days rose to 60 from 56 and CCC to 35 from 31, so the FY2025 stocking risk is not gone; a NWC return to the FY2025 11.7% of sales would take ~IDR2.8tn out of first-year FCFF.
challenges.answer: Bear rebuilt around the ASP reversal and a working-capital relapse: revenue growth multiplied by 0.65, gross margin -1.8pp, NWC intensity x1.3 toward the FY2025 peak; the bear now values the shares below the price.

challenges.challenge: The scenario framework cannot produce a loss case because no multiple is shocked: the worst cell of the section-4 sensitivity grid (revenue -4pp, GM -2pp every year) still values the shares at Rp685, above the Rp510 price. The bear narrative says "the multiple stays at book value" and the bull says the shares "re-rate toward quality multiples", but both shocks are operating only. A de-rating to the stock's own trough or the IDX premium de-rating base rate is the main downside and is absent.
challenges.answer: Both tails now shock the discount rate (bear +1pp, bull -1pp) as the de-rating channel the engine exposes, and the text states a multiple de-rating of the same size is the same trade; the bear is below the price.

challenges.challenge: ERAL (IDX: ERAL) is a separately listed subsidiary (279 stores, 18.1% GPM, +44.7% 9M26 sales, 16.4% ROIC) but the report never states ERAA's stake, never marks it at market, and shows no SOTP; the group is valued as one DCF and the minority deducted at book (1,542). If ERAL trades above the book value of the minority, ERAA's stake is worth more than the model shows; if below, the consolidated DCF overstates it. Either way it is a verifiable cross-check left out.
challenges.answer: ERAA's 80% stake in ERAL is now fact F40 and stated in section 1; the model deducts total minority at book while the market prices the minority we do not own, and the direction of that cross-check is stated in the valuation section.

challenges.challenge: The model has ERAA in IDR17.2tn of net cash by 2035 on a 30% payout and never returns it: no special dividend, buyback or payout step-up in the base or the bull, although the bull narrative explicitly claims "a higher payout" and the datapack's falling share count suggests a buyback is already running. The capital-return lever is the largest mitigant to the "cash-flow discount" thesis and is absent from the valuation.
challenges.answer: No buyback, special dividend or payout policy is disclosed in the LK; the falling vendor share count was the error corrected in C2, not a buyback. Base payout raised to the delivered 33% and the surplus cash is carried and flagged as upside, not invented into the target.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E interest expense is 799.0 on the FY2025 peak debt of 9,399.7 at 8.5%, while FY2025 actual interest was 549.5 and the 9M26 quarterly run-rate (422.3) annualises to ~563 on debt the report says fell 23%. Debt is held flat for ten years while net debt reaches -17,218, so the model charges loan interest forever and credits 2.6% on cash; this suppresses FY2026E NP by ~150 (~10%) with no source. The Q4 bridge compounds it: FY2026E NP of 1,442 implies Q4 of 354 against Q4 2025's 410 (-14%) after 9M +38.5%.
challenges.answer: Cost of debt cut to the 6.0% the 9M26 interest run-rate implies and net borrowing set to -1,175 so gross debt follows the 30 September balance of 8,224.6; FY2026 interest is no longer charged on peak debt.

challenges.challenge: Minority interest is forecast at 10% against 12.9% delivered in 9M26 (1,249 less 1,088), and applied to the full year it implies a negative Q4 minority (FY NP 1,602.6 less 9M actual 1,249 leaves 354 for Q4, equal to the model's Q4 NP to parent). ERAL grew 44.7% with a rising net margin, so its minority share should rise, not fall; "stabilises" is unsourced. The 10% assumption overstates FY2026E NP to parent by ~46 (3%).
challenges.answer: Minority interest held at the delivered 12.9% of net profit for every year, not 10%; NP to parent is rebuilt on that basis and the 9M-to-FY bridge follows the same share.

challenges.challenge: The earnings-quality defence does not reconcile. OCF 225.2 + interest 549.5 + cash tax 592.4 = 1,367, which is 56% of EBIT 2,435, not "close to operating profit"; only after adding back the 3,265 working-capital build does it reach EBITDA (4,632 vs 3,824), and that bridge is not shown. Section 3 also calls the 7,603 NWC balance a "one-off working-capital benefit" when the model's dNWC is -1,232. The 9M26 tax basis (24.5%, 405 on PBT 1,655) is cited to S6/S7 but appears in neither; it is the S0 datapack quarterly.
challenges.answer: The OCF-to-EBITDA bridge is now in the investment summary: OCF plus interest paid plus tax paid, with the working-capital build as the reconciling item; the NWC balance is corrected to the release from the FY2025 peak, and the 9M26 tax line is cited to the data pack.

challenges.challenge: The load-bearing 9M26 figures all come from a 21-page company investor presentation (S6), not the 9M2026 LK the live thesis says was published by 2026-10-31. S6 has no balance sheet, no cash-flow statement and no tax line, so the claim that the thesis's cash-conversion kill "is no longer failing" cannot be verified from it, and NWC of 7,603, net debt 4,582 and CCC 35 rest on a company summary. S3/S4/S5 are 2014-15 filings, unused, and still registered.
challenges.answer: The 9M26 balance-sheet items and tax charge are now cited to the data pack quarterly statement and the report says the filed 9M2026 LK is the next document wanted; the 2014-15 filings are not used in any number.

challenges.challenge: The report's own multiple cross-checks value the shares at Rp576/Rp606, +13%/+19%, and the stock already trades at 6.7x FY2025 earnings against ERAA's five-year mean of 6.45x; the +145% target is entirely the DCF, which is 3.5x the multiples. The reverse DCF's "-10.3% FY2027 revenue" presents as market pessimism what is equally a ~29% discount rate on the model's own cash flows (the price is reached at WACC ~29%). The rating survives a doubled bear only because the bear cannot fall below the price.
challenges.answer: The multiple-implied discount to the DCF is shown next to the DCF and the reverse-DCF growth language is removed: the price is presented as a discount rate and trust discount, which the engine cannot bracket as a growth rate.

challenges.challenge: The summary declares T-INDO-ERAA-001 superseded, but fund record still reads status live, PASS_REDUCED, entry 560, target 960, kill 420; the coverage report never reconciles Rp1,224 with the thesis's Rp960, nor the 560 entry/420 kill with the Rp510 price, and the cash-conversion claim cites S6 (no cash-flow statement). Prose supersession leaves two live views on one name.
challenges.answer: The investment summary now states that this coverage view governs the position, with its own target and rating, and that the thesis kill is only crossed below the current price; the thesis file sits with the INDO desk and is not ours to edit.

challenges.challenge: House macro is read (IDR 18,350, BI 5.75, CPI 3.28, consumer discretionary AVOID) but gross margin is held at 11.4-11.7% to 2035 versus FY2025's 10.9% with dollar-invoiced COGS and no FX pass-through assumption or sensitivity; the report's own risk section says 100bp is the buffer, while a 10% IDR move on ~70% imported COGS is several times that. The CPI is rendered as "328.0%" in sections 2 and 5, and the deck's AVOID stance does not change the base case.
challenges.answer: The gross-margin basis now states an explicit one-quarter FX pass-through assumption tied to the house IDR path, the sensitivity grid is named as the pass-through stress, and the CPI placeholder renders 3.3% instead of 328.0%.

challenges.challenge: Inputs disagree across report, basis and model: capex is "1.4% of sales" in section 3, "held at 1.15%" in the basis and 1.35% in the model; terminal growth is 3.0% in the input but "4% growth" in params_basis; cost of debt is 8.5% in the input and 9.45% in the WACC; tax is 25% in the model and 22% in the WACC; the restatement "lifts historical EBIT by roughly a third" when it is +47.5% (1,650.4 to 2,434.7). Rendered text carries "IDR IDR2,434.7bnbn", "2,655 stores stores", "15,950 million sharesm" and "IDR IDR65,768,805,930.2bn".
challenges.answer: Inputs reconciled to one number each: terminal capex 2.3% and g 3% everywhere, the WACC's 9.45% debt cost and 22% shield distinguished from the P&L's 6.0% and 25%, the restatement stated as almost half, and currency/unit renderings fixed.

challenges.challenge: The summary OCF bridge says the LK shows IDR541.1bn of tax inside operating cash flow. 541.1 is the P&L tax expense; the LK cash-flow statement shows income taxes paid of IDR592.35bn [S7]. The bridge understates cash tax by IDR51.3bn and the reconciles-rather-than-exposes conclusion rests on the wrong number.
challenges.answer: Replaced the P&L charge with the cash-flow line. Added fact F55, income taxes paid of IDR592.350786bn from the AR2025 consolidated cash-flow statement ("Pajak penghasilan ( 592.350.786)", p.165) [S7]. The investment-summary bridge now adds OCF 225.2 + interest paid 549.5 + tax paid 592.4 and shows the P&L charge of 541.1 only as the charge it is, with the residual gap to EBITDA of 3,823.7 stated as the working-capital build. The same correction is carried into section 3 [S7].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says the model books a cash inflow in the first year that reverses to an outflow from FY2027. Model FCFF is +IDR1,869.8bn in FY2027E and +IDR2,117.7bn in FY2028E; only the working-capital release reverses. As written the reader is told the DCF has negative mid-period cash.
